The teacher-checked set includes at least one weaker source on purpose (an advertisement, a rumor-filled news report), so judging credibility has something to judge; digital sources are a fenced set of stable public pages, with no open search.

words: analysis; reflection; evidence; response; routine; draft
notes: Drawing evidence from literary and informational texts to support analysis, reflection and research (W.6.9; W.6.9a and b apply the grade 6 reading standards, for example comparing genres or tracing an argument), and writing routinely over both long and short time frames (W.6.10). This is the daily written question on the day's text and the one-sitting evidence paragraph: point, quoted evidence, explanation. Grade 5 drew evidence the same way at grade 5 demand; grade 6 applies it to grade 6 reading standards. Practised on every reading day. Limit: one piece of evidence per point; several pieces per point are grade 7.

words: discussion; prepare; evidence; role; paraphrase; perspective; build on
notes: Taking part in discussions one-on-one, in groups and teacher-led on grade 6 texts and topics: come prepared and cite the text (SL.6.1a), follow agreed rules, set goals and deadlines, take roles (b), ask and answer with elaboration (c), and review key ideas, showing other views through reflection and paraphrase (d). Grade 5 asked the same with less independence; grade 6 adds setting goals and deadlines and paraphrasing several perspectives. A taught routine with sentence frames that fade across the year; a formal text discussion at least every two weeks. Limit: understanding others' views; changing one's own view on new information is grade 7.

words: present; claim; finding; eye contact; volume; multimedia; formal English
notes: Presenting claims and findings in a logical order with pertinent facts and details, with eye contact, adequate volume and clear speech (SL.6.4); adding graphics, images or sound to clarify (SL.6.5); and adapting speech to the setting, using formal English when it fits (SL.6.6). Grade 5 reported on a topic in order; grade 6 presents claims and findings and adds adapting register to the context. Two or three short talks a year, each tied to a research project or argument from the unit. Limit: sequencing ideas logically; emphasising salient points in a focused way is grade 7.

words: pronoun; subjective; objective; possessive; intensive; antecedent; shift
notes: Using pronouns correctly in writing and speech: proper case (L.6.1a), intensive pronouns (b), no shifts in pronoun number and person (c), no vague pronouns with unclear antecedents (d), and recognising variations from standard English in one's own and others' writing and speaking, with strategies to improve conventional expression (e). Grade 5 worked on conjunctions and verb tense; grade 6 is the pronoun year. Taught in short openers on sentences from the anchor texts and the student's own drafts, then applied in editing. Teacher note: L.6.1e is taught as recognising variations in examples of one's own and others' writing and speech, explaining which form fits a named setting, and using a model, reference or checklist to revise chosen examples into conventional English; home language and dialects are respected and never corrected as wrong in themselves. Most of the teaching happens in the revise days of a process piece, on pronouns in the students' own drafts, rather than in stand-alone grammar days: grammar taught apart from writing does little for writing (Writing Next, 2007).

words: comma; parentheses; dash; nonrestrictive; parenthetical; spell
notes: Using commas, parentheses and dashes to set off nonrestrictive and parenthetical elements (L.6.2a) and spelling correctly (L.6.2b), with spelling of long words taught through word parts. Grade 5 used commas after introductory elements and in a series; grade 6 adds the three ways to set off an extra element and when each fits. Model sentences come from the anchor texts; practised in editing. Limit: setting off elements; commas between coordinate adjectives are grade 7, and dashes and ellipses for a pause or omission are grade 8. Teacher note: the dash is taught because the standard asks for it; a dash appears only in the exercise sentences students punctuate and in the texts they read; Curio Class's own prose stays free of em dashes (Cory, 2026-11-13).

words: context; root; affix; Greek; Latin; dictionary; verify; cause and effect; part and whole
notes: Working out unknown and multiple-meaning words from grade 6 reading by choosing among strategies: context (L.6.4a), Greek and Latin affixes and roots (b, for example aud in audience, auditory, audible), print and digital reference works for pronunciation, meaning and part of speech (c), and checking the guess in context or a dictionary (d). L.6.5b sits here: using word relationships (cause and effect, part and whole, item and category) to understand each word. Grade 5 used affixes and roots and reference works; grade 6 adds verifying the first guess and choosing flexibly. Practised on words the unit's texts supply. Limit: common roots; less common roots and specialised references are grade 7.

words: cite; several; evidence; inference; analysis; support
notes: Citing several pieces of textual evidence to support an analysis of what a text says explicitly and what it implies, in literature and literary nonfiction. Grade 6 cited evidence for a point; grade 7 asks for several pieces gathered across the text, so the reader must look beyond the first line that fits. Practised on every anchor of the year, now including longer stories, a short play and longer articles in the middle of the grades 6 to 8 band. RL.7.1 and RI.7.1 share the row because the skill is the same; RI.7.1 adds evidence from data displays. Limit: several pieces; choosing the strongest is grade 8.

words: theme; develop; over the course of; objective summary; shift
notes: Determining a theme and analysing how it develops over the course of a text, and writing an objective summary. Grade 6 found a theme and the details that convey it; grade 7 follows the theme as it grows, turns or deepens from beginning to end (where it is first hinted, where it is tested, where it lands). The summary is now called objective. Practised on original stories of 2,500 to 6,000 words and on the year's long text. Limit: development across the text; its relationship to characters, setting and plot together is grade 8.

words: setting; character; plot; interact; shape; influence; motive
notes: Analysing how particular elements of a story or drama interact, for example how setting shapes characters or plot, or how a character's choice changes the setting. Grade 6 described plot episodes and character change; grade 7 asks how one element acts on another. Practised on original stories where place matters (a flood town, a city summer, a ranch in drought) and the year's short original play. Limit: how elements act on each other; how a single line of dialogue or incident propels the action is grade 8.

words: rhyme; alliteration; repetition; connotation; allusion; tone; stanza
cross_subject: social-studies:ss7-greek-myth (mythological allusions met in the grade 7 myth unit)
notes: Determining figurative and connotative meanings and analysing the impact of rhymes and other repeated sounds (alliteration, repetition) on a verse, stanza or section of a story or drama. Grade 6 analysed one word choice's impact on tone; grade 7 adds sound. L.7.5 sits here: L.7.5a interpreting figures of speech including literary, biblical and mythological allusions in context, and L.7.5c connotation (refined, polite, condescending); L.7.5b is owned by e7-word-strategies. Practised on original poems read aloud and silently, and on a few short public-domain poems as paired reads. Limit: sound and word; analogies and allusions as word choice in prose are grade 8.

words: form; soliloquy; sonnet; stage direction; line; meaning; structure
notes: Analysing how a drama's or poem's form or structure contributes to its meaning: what a soliloquy lets the audience hear, how a sonnet's turn changes the argument, how stage directions carry what dialogue does not. Grade 6 analysed how one part fits the whole; grade 7 asks what the form itself does. Practised on an original short play with a soliloquy and on original sonnets and fixed-form poems, with one older public-domain sonnet as a paired read (BASELINE rule 29). Limit: one form at a time; comparing the structures of two texts is grade 8.

words: point of view; narrator; character; contrast; perspective; alternating
notes: Analysing how an author develops and contrasts the points of view of different characters or narrators, for example a story told in alternating chapters by two siblings. Grade 6 explained how one narrator's view is built; grade 7 sets two or more views against each other and asks how the author makes the difference. The point-of-view model gains a second column. Practised on original stories with two narrators or with a narrator whose view clashes with another character's, 2,000 to 5,000 words. Limit: contrast among characters; the gap between characters and the reader (dramatic irony) is grade 8.

words: medium; version; technique; lighting; sound; camera angle; delivery
notes: Comparing a written story, drama, poem or nonfiction text with its audio, filmed, staged or multimedia version, analysing the effects of techniques unique to each medium (lighting, sound, colour, camera angle; for a speech, how delivery changes the impact of the words). RL.7.7 and RI.7.7 share the row: the same analysis in literature and in nonfiction. Grade 6 compared the experience of reading and watching; grade 7 names the medium's own techniques and their effects. Practised on a scene of the year's original play recorded for the course, and on a public-domain recorded speech with its transcript. Limit: analysing effects; judging how faithful a production is and the director's choices is grade 8. Teacher note: recordings are made for the course or in the public domain.

words: historical fiction; account; portrayal; period; alter; accurate
cross_subject: social-studies:ss7-athenian-democracy (a story set in the Athenian assembly read beside a historical account)
notes: Comparing a fictional portrayal of a time, place or character with a historical account of the same period, to understand how fiction writers use or change history. Grade 6 compared texts in different genres on a theme; grade 7 sets fiction against history and asks what the writer kept, invented and changed, and why. Practised on an original historical story with a historical account of the same period: for example a story set in the Athenian assembly with a short account of Athenian democracy (joining the grade 7 social studies year), or a story of a 1930s dust storm with recent public-domain government accounts. Each text 800 to 3,000 words. Limit: one portrayal and one account.

words: stamina; reread; complex; long text; independent reading; log
cross_subject: social-studies:ss7-athenian-democracy (the citizens knowledge thread); science:s7-ecosystem-disruption (the human impact knowledge thread)
notes: Reading and understanding literature and literary nonfiction in the grades 6 to 8 complexity band by the end of the year, with support at the high end. The standard's wording does not change from grade 6; the demand climbs through the texts (a working split, ours: grade 7 anchors centred in the middle of the band, more at its top with support) and the volume (one long text read whole, longer anchors, independent reading with a log and conferences). RL.7.10 and RI.7.10 share the row; the year's anchors aim at about 55 percent informational. Knowledge thread (topic sets that build across grades 6 to 8; the course frame makes the final pick of texts). Thread 1, citizens and government in Greece: inherited from grade 6 law codes (e6-reading-range); grade 7 adds Athenian democracy and who counted as a citizen, beside social studies ss7-athenian-democracy and ss7-greek-myth; words reused: law, code, justice, with citizen and democracy added (Rome stays with social studies ss7-roman-republic; ELA grade 7 reads no Roman text); used again in e8-reading-range (founding documents). Thread 2, ecosystems, resources and human impact: inherited from grade 6 Earth systems and hazards (e6-reading-range); grade 7 adds how populations, resource use and climate change disturb ecosystems, beside science s7-ecosystem-disruption, s7-population-consumption and s7-climate-change-evidence; words reused: system, data, evidence, with population, resource and impact added; used again in e8-reading-range (science claims in public life).

words: central idea; develop; objective summary; supporting detail; media; clarify
notes: Determining two or more central ideas in a text and analysing their development over the course of the text, and writing an objective summary. SL.7.2 sits here: analysing the main ideas and details in information presented in diverse media and formats (a narrated graph, a short recorded explainer) and how they clarify the topic. Grade 6 found one central idea and the details that convey it; grade 7 tracks two or more as they develop. Practised on longer informational articles (1,200 to 3,000 words) and chapters of a nonfiction book, plus one media source per unit. Limit: development of the ideas; their relationship to supporting ideas in detail is grade 8.

words: interaction; influence; individual; event; idea; cause
notes: Analysing the interactions between individuals, events and ideas in a text: how an idea moves people to act, or how a person changes the course of events or ideas. Grade 6 followed one individual, event or idea through a text; grade 7 asks how they act on each other. Practised on history and science narratives: a biography chapter of a scientist, an account of how a public health idea spread, 1,000 to 3,000 words. Limit: interactions; the connections and distinctions an author draws through comparisons, analogies and categories are grade 8.

words: word choice; tone; connotation; technical; domain-specific; impact
notes: Determining figurative, connotative and technical meanings in informational text and analysing the impact of a specific word choice on meaning and tone (an article that calls a plan 'bold' and another that calls it 'reckless'). L.7.6 sits here: the unit's general academic and domain words, drawn from these texts and returned to. Grade 6 determined meanings; grade 7 adds the impact of word choice on tone in nonfiction, as RL.6.4 did in literature. Practised on the unit's informational anchors. Limit: one word choice's impact; analogies and allusions as word choice are grade 8.

words: structure; organize; major section; whole; develop; heading
notes: Analysing the structure an author uses to organise a text, including how the major sections contribute to the whole and to the development of the ideas. Grade 6 analysed how one part fits; grade 7 looks at the whole design (why a report goes problem, history, three cases, recommendation). Practised on longer reports and nonfiction chapters with sections, 1,500 to 3,500 words, often recent public-domain government reports. Limit: the major sections; the role of each sentence in a single paragraph is grade 8.

words: position; point of view; purpose; distinguish; others; counter
notes: Determining an author's point of view or purpose and analysing how the author distinguishes their position from that of others ('some argue that...; but the data show...'). Grade 6 explained how one author's view is conveyed; grade 7 adds how the author sets that view apart from others'. Practised on opinion essays and argumentative articles that name another view, original or recent public-domain, 600 to 2,000 words. Limit: distinguishing positions; how an author acknowledges and answers conflicting evidence is grade 8.

words: reasoning; sound; relevant; sufficient; evidence; evaluate
cross_subject: science:s7-climate-change-evidence (apply argument evaluation to the climate knowledge thread)
notes: Tracing and evaluating the argument and specific claims in a text, judging whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence relevant and sufficient. SL.7.3 sits here: the same evaluation of a speaker's argument. Grade 6 sorted supported from unsupported claims; grade 7 asks whether the support is enough and whether the reasoning holds. The argument-map gains a mark for each link (sound or not) and each evidence box (relevant, sufficient). Practised on editorials, public comment letters and recorded speeches, 500 to 1,500 words. Limit: soundness and sufficiency; recognising when irrelevant evidence is brought in is grade 8.

words: emphasise; interpretation; key information; shape; author; topic
notes: Analysing how two or more authors writing on the same topic shape their presentations of key information by stressing different evidence or advancing different interpretations of facts. Grade 6 compared one author's presentation of events with another's; grade 7 asks how each author's choices of evidence and interpretation shape the reader's understanding. Practised on paired articles on one unit topic (for example two accounts of a city's response to an epidemic), each 600 to 2,000 words. Limit: different emphasis and interpretation; texts that conflict on matters of fact are grade 8.

words: claim; opposing claim; acknowledge; logical; cohesion; credible; accurate
notes: Writing arguments: introduce the claim and acknowledge alternate or opposing claims, organising reasons and evidence logically (W.7.1a); support with logical reasoning and relevant evidence from accurate, credible sources (b); create cohesion among claim, reasons and evidence (c); formal style (d); a conclusion that follows from and supports the argument (e). Grade 6 organised one claim's reasons clearly; grade 7 adds acknowledging opposing claims, logical reasoning and cohesion. Two pieces a year, one through the full process. Limit: acknowledging the other side; distinguishing one's claim from it and handling counterclaims is grade 8.

words: preview; cohesion; transition; definition; classification; precise
notes: Writing informative and explanatory texts: introduce the topic clearly and preview what follows, organising by definition, classification, comparison or cause and effect with headings and graphics (W.7.2a); develop with facts and quotations (b); transitions that create cohesion (c); precise and domain words (d); formal style (e); a conclusion that follows and supports (f). Grade 6 used transitions to clarify; grade 7 adds a preview and cohesion. Two to three pieces a year on the unit's topic. Limit: organising strategies named in the standard; organising into broader categories is grade 8.

words: point of view; narrator; pacing; capture; reflect; conclusion
notes: Writing narratives: establish a context and a point of view and introduce the narrator and characters (W.7.3a); use dialogue, pacing and description (b); transitions for sequence and shifts (c); precise, sensory language that captures the action (d); and a conclusion that reflects on the events (e). Grade 6 introduced a narrator; grade 7 adds establishing a point of view on purpose, capturing action and reflecting in the ending. Model texts are the unit's two-narrator stories. Two pieces a year. Limit: reflection in the conclusion; reflection as a technique inside the narrative is grade 8.

words: task; purpose; audience; link; cite; publish; collaborate
notes: Producing clear, coherent writing fitted to task, purpose and audience (W.7.4), and using technology to produce and publish writing, linking to and citing sources, and collaborating (W.7.6). Grade 6 published and typed three pages; grade 7 adds linking to and citing sources in published work. Practised on every process piece; one piece a year is published with live links to its sources. Teacher note: a room without devices prints its pieces with a source list; that supports citing but does not demonstrate linking to sources (W.7.6). The linked piece is made on a shared classroom device or in a lab session in the school day, or W.7.6 is recorded as unfinished for that class.

words: revise; purpose; audience; concise; wordiness; redundancy; precise
notes: Strengthening writing with some guidance and support by planning, revising, editing, rewriting or trying a new approach, now focusing on how well purpose and audience have been served (W.7.5), with editing up to grade 7 conventions. L.7.3 sits here: choosing language that is precise and concise and cutting wordiness and redundancy (L.7.3a). Grade 6 revised for clarity and consistent style; grade 7 adds revising against purpose and audience and cutting wordiness. Editing applies the grade 6 pronoun work. Each process piece has a named feedback step.

words: search term; accuracy; credibility; citation format; related question; investigate
cross_subject: social-studies:ss7-research-greek (judging credible and relevant sources in a research task)
notes: Conducting short research projects from several sources and generating further related, focused questions (W.7.7), and gathering information with effective search terms, judging the credibility and accuracy of each source, quoting or paraphrasing without plagiarism, and following a standard citation format (W.7.8). Grade 6 refocused the question, judged credibility and gave basic bibliographic information; grade 7 adds search terms, accuracy, new questions and a standard format. Two or three projects a year on the unit's topic. Limit: questions given or chosen from a list; a self-generated question with several avenues is grade 8.

words: analysis; reflection; evidence; several; response; routine
notes: Drawing evidence from texts for analysis, reflection and research, applying the grade 7 reading standards (W.7.9a, for example fiction against history; W.7.9b, evaluating an argument), and writing routinely over long and short time frames (W.7.10). The daily written question and the one-sitting evidence paragraph now use several pieces of evidence. Grade 6 applied grade 6 reading standards with one piece per point; grade 7 applies grade 7 standards with several. Practised on every reading day.

words: prepare; research; elaborate; on topic; acknowledge; modify; view
notes: Discussions on grade 7 texts and topics: come prepared, having read or researched (SL.7.1a); follow rules, track progress toward goals and deadlines (b); ask questions that draw out elaboration and bring talk back on topic (c); acknowledge new information and, when warranted, change one's own view (d). Grade 6 set goals and paraphrased others; grade 7 adds tracking progress, steering back to the topic and modifying one's view. A formal text discussion at least every two weeks, frames faded further than in grade 6.

words: salient; focused; coherent; emphasise; multimedia; formal English
notes: Presenting claims and findings, emphasising salient points in a focused, coherent way with pertinent details and examples (SL.7.4); multimedia and visual displays that clarify claims and emphasise salient points (SL.7.5); adapting speech to context with formal English when it fits (SL.7.6). Grade 6 sequenced ideas logically; grade 7 asks the speaker to choose and stress what matters most. Two or three talks a year tied to research or argument.

words: phrase; clause; simple; compound; complex; compound-complex; modifier; dangling
notes: Explaining what phrases and clauses do in general and in particular sentences (L.7.1a), choosing among simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences to show relationships among ideas (b), and placing phrases and clauses well, fixing misplaced and dangling modifiers (c). Grade 6 varied sentence patterns in revision; grade 7 names the parts and chooses sentence types on purpose. Taught through sentence combining on anchor-text sentences, applied in drafts. Limit: phrases and clauses; verbals and verb voice and mood are grade 8.

words: coordinate adjective; comma; spell
notes: Using a comma between coordinate adjectives (a fascinating, enjoyable film; but not an old green shirt) and spelling correctly (L.7.2a and b). Grade 6 set off nonrestrictive elements; grade 7 adds the test for coordinate adjectives (can the order switch and 'and' go between?). Spelling of long words continues through word parts. Practised in openers and editing.

words: root; affix; specialised; reference; synonym; antonym; analogy; verify
cross_subject: social-studies:ss7-latin-legacy (Latin roots, prefixes and suffixes)
notes: Working out unknown and multiple-meaning words from grade 7 reading: context (L.7.4a), Greek and Latin roots and affixes (b, for example bell in belligerent, bellicose, rebel), general and specialised reference works (c), and checking the guess (d). L.7.5b sits here: synonym, antonym and analogy relationships to understand each word. Grade 6 used common references; grade 7 adds specialised references and analogy. Practised on words from the unit's texts.

words: strongest; evidence; cite; analysis; inference; weigh
notes: Citing the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what a text says explicitly and what it implies. Grade 7 gathered several pieces; grade 8 asks the reader to weigh them and choose the strongest, saying why it beats the others. Practised on every anchor, now at the high end of the grades 6 to 8 band. RL.8.1 and RI.8.1 share the row; RI.8.1 adds weighing data against testimony.

words: theme; relationship; character; setting; plot; objective summary
notes: Determining a theme and analysing its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to the characters, setting and plot, and writing an objective summary. Grade 7 tracked a theme's development; grade 8 ties that development to what the characters do, where they are and what happens. Practised on original stories and novella chapters of 3,000 to 8,000 words and the year's long text.

words: dialogue; incident; propel; reveal; provoke; decision
notes: Analysing how particular lines of dialogue or incidents propel the action, reveal a character or provoke a decision. Grade 7 analysed how story elements act on each other; grade 8 zooms to the single line or incident that moves the story. Practised on original stories and the year's original play, where a short exchange turns the plot.

words: analogy; allusion; irony; pun; connotation; tone; word choice
notes: Determining figurative and connotative meanings and analysing the impact of word choices on meaning and tone, including analogies and allusions to other texts. L.8.5 sits here: L.8.5a verbal irony and puns in context, L.8.5c connotation (bullheaded, willful, firm, resolute); L.8.5b is owned by e8-word-strategies. Grade 7 added sound; grade 8 adds analogy, allusion and irony. Practised on original stories and poems that allude to texts read in earlier units or grades (a myth, a well-known speech).

words: structure; compare; meaning; style; frame; chronology
notes: Comparing and contrasting the structure of two or more texts and analysing how each structure contributes to its meaning and style (a story told in order against one told in reverse; a poem in free verse against one in a fixed form on the same subject). Grade 7 analysed what one form does; grade 8 sets two structures side by side. Practised on paired original texts on one unit topic, each 500 to 3,000 words.

words: dramatic irony; suspense; humour; audience; reader; point of view
notes: Analysing how differences between what characters know and what the audience or reader knows (dramatic irony) create suspense or humour. Grade 7 contrasted characters' points of view; grade 8 adds the reader as a party to the point-of-view model. Practised on the year's original play and on original mystery and comic stories. Hands on to e9-rl-world-stories: grades 9 and 10 turn RL.6 to cultural point of view. Grade 11 (e11-lit-irony) comes back to dramatic irony with a short retrieval and reteach, not as an assumed skill.

words: production; faithful; depart; director; actor; interpretation; script
notes: Analysing how far a filmed or live production of a story or drama stays faithful to or departs from the text or script, and evaluating the choices the director or actors made. Grade 7 analysed techniques unique to each medium; grade 8 judges the production's choices against the text. Practised on the year's original play, staged by the class in two versions, and on a course-made recording. Teacher note: recordings are made for the course or in the public domain.

words: myth; traditional story; character type; pattern; archetype; rendered new
cross_subject: social-studies:ss7-greek-myth (Greek myths met in grade 7)
notes: Analysing how a modern work of fiction draws on themes, patterns of events or character types from myths and traditional stories, and how the material is made new. Grade 7 compared fiction with history; grade 8 compares a modern story with its old source. Practised on an original modern story built on a myth or folktale, with the traditional story (public domain) as the paired read (BASELINE rule 29). Teacher note: the standard names religious works such as the Bible as one possible source ('such as', not required); the pick, open with the lead, is myths and folktales as the sources, with no religious work as an anchor; any religious text used is read as literature and no student is asked to state a belief.

words: independent; complex; long text; stamina; log
cross_subject: social-studies:ss8-declaration (the founding documents knowledge thread); science:s8-human-trait-technology (the science claims knowledge thread)
notes: Reading and understanding literature and literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 6 to 8 band independently and proficiently by the end of the year. Grade 7 read in the band with support at the high end; grade 8 fades routine support at the top as students show readiness: the year's later anchors include independent reading checkpoints at the high end without before-reading help, while targeted instruction and access supports continue for students who need them, and supported reading is kept apart from evidence of independent proficiency. One long text read whole, longer anchors, independent reading with a log and conferences. RL.8.10 and RI.8.10 share the row; the anchors aim at about 55 percent informational. Knowledge thread (topic sets that build across grades 6 to 8; the course frame makes the final pick of texts). Thread 1, founding documents and rights: inherited from grade 7 Athens (e7-reading-range); grade 8 adds the Declaration, the Constitution, its amendments and a free press, beside social studies ss8-greek-roman-roots, ss8-declaration and ss8-press-freedom; words reused: citizen, democracy, law, with right, press, constitution and amendment added (the republic is met through social studies ss8-greek-roman-roots, not ELA grade 7); used again in e9-ri-purpose-rhetoric (seminal U.S. documents). Thread 2, science claims in public life: inherited from grade 7 human impact and data (e7-reading-range); grade 8 adds heredity, technology that changes traits, and judging science claims in the news, beside science s8-human-trait-technology and social studies ss8-news-literacy; words reused: data, evidence, population, impact, with trait, gene, source, claim and trial added; used again in e9-ri-argument-evaluate (judging data claims).

words: central idea; supporting idea; develop; objective summary; relationship
notes: Determining a central idea and analysing its development over the text, including its relationship to supporting ideas, and writing an objective summary. Grade 7 tracked two or more central ideas; grade 8 asks how the supporting ideas build, limit or qualify the central one. Practised on long articles, report chapters and essays of 1,500 to 4,000 words.

words: connection; distinction; analogy; comparison; category
notes: Analysing how a text makes connections among and distinctions between individuals, ideas or events, through comparisons, analogies or categories (an explainer that compares the bloodstream to a road network; a history that sorts reformers into groups). Grade 7 analysed interactions; grade 8 asks how the author's comparisons and categories make the links. Practised on science and history explainers and essays, 1,000 to 3,000 words.

words: word choice; analogy; allusion; tone; technical; domain-specific
notes: Determining figurative, connotative and technical meanings in informational text and analysing the impact of word choices on meaning and tone, including analogies and allusions to other texts (a speech that echoes a founding document). L.8.6 sits here: the unit's general academic and domain words from these texts. Grade 7 analysed one word choice's impact; grade 8 adds analogy and allusion in nonfiction. Practised on speeches, essays and articles, recent public-domain or original.

words: paragraph; sentence; role; develop; refine; key concept
notes: Analysing in detail the structure of one paragraph, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept (the sentence that defines, the one that limits, the one that gives the case). Grade 7 analysed how major sections build the whole; grade 8 works at sentence level inside a paragraph. Practised on dense paragraphs from science and history texts and from essays, 100 to 300 words each, reread several times.

words: acknowledge; respond; conflicting; viewpoint; concede; rebut
notes: Determining an author's point of view or purpose and analysing how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints (concede, then rebut; answer an objection with data). Grade 7 analysed how an author distinguishes a position from others; grade 8 asks how the author answers them. Practised on argumentative essays and public letters that take on an objection, original or recent public-domain, 800 to 2,500 words.

words: medium; advantage; disadvantage; motive; commercial; political; purpose
cross_subject: social-studies:ss8-news-literacy (judging news and advertising sources)
notes: Evaluating the advantages and disadvantages of different mediums (print or digital text, video, multimedia) for a topic or idea (RI.8.7), and analysing the purpose of information presented in diverse media and evaluating the social, commercial or political motives behind it (SL.8.2). Grade 7 analysed each medium's portrayal of a subject; grade 8 judges which medium serves the purpose and why the presenter chose it. Practised on one topic shown in a print article, a short video and an infographic made for the course, and on public notices and advertisements written for the course. Teacher note: no real brand or company appears; advertisements are written for the course.

words: delineate; irrelevant; sound; sufficient; relevant; reasoning
cross_subject: social-studies:ss8-editorial-analysis (claims and evidence in editorials)
notes: Delineating and evaluating the argument and claims in a text, judging soundness and the relevance and sufficiency of evidence, and recognising when irrelevant evidence is introduced (RI.8.8). SL.8.3 sits here: the same on a speaker's argument. Grade 7 judged soundness and sufficiency; grade 8 adds catching irrelevant evidence. Practised on editorials, public hearing testimony and recorded speeches, 600 to 2,000 words.

words: conflict; fact; interpretation; disagree; source; verify
notes: Analysing a case in which two or more texts give conflicting information on the same topic and identifying where they disagree on matters of fact or of interpretation. Grade 7 analysed how authors stress different evidence; grade 8 sorts real factual conflict from differing interpretation and asks which can be checked. Practised on paired or triple texts on one unit topic (two accounts of a historical event, two reports with different figures), each 500 to 2,000 words.

words: counterclaim; distinguish; rebut; cohesion; logical; credible
cross_subject: social-studies:ss8-civic-action (a proposal argued to an audience)
notes: Writing arguments: introduce the claim, acknowledge and distinguish it from alternate or opposing claims, and organise reasons and evidence logically (W.8.1a); logical reasoning and relevant evidence from accurate, credible sources (b); cohesion among claims, counterclaims, reasons and evidence (c); formal style (d); a conclusion that follows and supports (e). Grade 7 acknowledged opposing claims; grade 8 distinguishes the claim from them and works counterclaims into the argument. Two pieces a year, one through the full process.

words: broader category; well-chosen; varied transition; cohesion; preview
notes: Writing informative and explanatory texts: introduce and preview, organising ideas into broader categories with headings and graphics (W.8.2a); develop with relevant, well-chosen facts and quotations (b); varied transitions for cohesion (c); precise and domain words (d); formal style (e); a conclusion that follows and supports (f). Grade 7 used the named strategies and cohesion; grade 8 adds broader categories, well-chosen evidence and varied transitions. Two to three pieces a year on the unit's topic.

words: reflection; relationship; point of view; pacing; time frame
notes: Writing narratives: context and point of view (W.8.3a); dialogue, pacing, description and reflection (b); transitions that show the relationships among experiences and events, not just their order (c); precise, sensory language (d); a conclusion that reflects (e). Grade 7 reflected in the ending; grade 8 makes reflection a technique inside the narrative and links events by meaning. Model texts include the year's modern myth retellings. Two pieces a year, one through the full process.

words: task; purpose; audience; present; efficient; publish
notes: Producing clear, coherent writing fitted to task, purpose and audience (W.8.4), and using technology to produce and publish writing and present the relationships between information and ideas efficiently, and to collaborate (W.8.6). Grade 7 linked and cited sources; grade 8 adds presenting how ideas relate (a linked page, a diagram, a table) efficiently. Teacher note: without devices, the relationships are shown on paper with a hand-drawn diagram; that supports the thinking but does not demonstrate using technology to present them (W.8.6). The digital piece is made on a shared classroom device or in a lab session in the school day, or W.8.6 is recorded as unfinished for that class.

words: revise; purpose; audience; active voice; passive voice; mood; effect
notes: Strengthening writing with some guidance and support, focusing on purpose and audience (W.8.5), with editing up to grade 8 conventions. L.8.3 sits here: using active and passive voice and conditional and subjunctive mood for effect (stressing the actor or the action; expressing doubt or a state contrary to fact). The W.8.5 wording is the same as grade 7; the climb is in the conventions edited (grades 6 to 8) and the L.8.3 choices, and in longer pieces. Each process piece has a named feedback step.

words: self-generated question; avenue; search term; accuracy; citation format
cross_subject: social-studies:ss8-court-research (a research question answered from court and news sources)
notes: Conducting short research projects to answer a question, including one the student generates, and generating focused questions that open several avenues (W.8.7), with W.8.8 as in grade 7 (search terms, credibility and accuracy, quoting and paraphrasing, a standard citation format). Grade 7 generated related questions; grade 8 adds the student's own question and several avenues of exploration; the W.8.8 wording is unchanged from grade 7 and the climb is in source range and independence. Two or three projects a year, the last a student-chosen question on the unit topic.

words: analysis; reflection; strongest evidence; response; routine
notes: Drawing evidence from texts for analysis, reflection and research, applying grade 8 reading standards (W.8.9a, a modern story and its myth; W.8.9b, delineating an argument), and writing routinely over long and short time frames (W.8.10). The daily written question and the one-sitting evidence paragraph now choose the strongest evidence. Grade 7 used several pieces; grade 8 chooses and defends the best.

words: decision-making; connect; qualify; justify; evidence; several speakers
notes: Discussions on grade 8 texts and topics: come prepared (SL.8.1a); rules for discussion and decision-making, tracking goals and deadlines (b); questions that connect the ideas of several speakers, answering with evidence (c); acknowledging new information and qualifying or justifying one's own view in light of evidence (d). Grade 7 modified views and kept talk on topic; grade 8 adds group decision-making, connecting several speakers and qualifying a view. Student-led formal discussions at least every two weeks, frames mostly gone.

words: valid reasoning; relevant evidence; integrate; multimedia; formal English
notes: Presenting claims and findings with salient points in a focused way, relevant evidence, sound valid reasoning and well-chosen details (SL.8.4); integrating multimedia and visual displays to clarify, strengthen claims and add interest (SL.8.5); adapting speech to context (SL.8.6). Grade 7 stressed salient points; grade 8 adds sound reasoning and integrated, not added, media. Two or three talks a year, one a formal argument to an audience beyond the class where possible.

words: verbal; gerund; participle; infinitive; active; passive; mood; subjunctive
notes: Explaining the function of verbals (gerunds, participles, infinitives) in general and in particular sentences (L.8.1a), forming and using active and passive voice (b) and the indicative, imperative, interrogative, conditional and subjunctive moods (c), and fixing shifts in voice and mood (d). Grade 7 named phrases and clauses; grade 8 adds verbals (phrases built on verb forms), voice and mood. Taught on anchor sentences and applied in drafts.

words: comma; ellipsis; dash; pause; break; omission; spell
notes: Using a comma, ellipsis or dash to show a pause or break (L.8.2a), an ellipsis to mark an omission in a quotation (b), and spelling correctly (c). Grade 7 used commas between coordinate adjectives; grade 8 adds the pause and the omission, used when quoting evidence. Teacher note: the dash is taught because the standard asks for it; a dash appears only in the exercise sentences students punctuate and in the texts they read; Curio Class's own prose stays free of em dashes (Cory, 2026-11-13).

words: root; affix; context; reference; verify; word relationship
notes: Working out unknown and multiple-meaning words from grade 8 reading: context (L.8.4a), Greek and Latin roots and affixes (b, for example cede in precede, recede, secede), general and specialised references (c), and checking the guess (d). L.8.5b sits here: using relationships between words to understand each. The wording barely changes from grade 7; the climb is in the roots and the texts. Practised on words from the unit's texts.

words: textual evidence; explicit; inference; thorough; quotation; lead-in
notes: Cite strong and thorough evidence for what a story says outright and for what a reader infers. Grade 8 asked for the single piece that most strongly supports a reading; 9-10 adds thorough: several pieces, explicit and inferred, gathered into one reading, each quotation led in and explained. Practised on short stories of 2,000 to 6,000 words (for example Poe, Maupassant, Saki, London) and on the year's play. Grade 9 takes it to two or three well-chosen quotations per claim with the inference said in the student's words, with a teacher model first and an evidence chart that fades by midyear. Grade 10 carries it across a whole novel. Text demand for English 9: anchors in the grades 9-10 band (2012 supplement to Appendix A: about 1050 to 1335 Lexile), most placed in the lower two thirds, with scaffolding at the high end; a poem or play has no usable measure and rests on the qualitative read.

words: theme; central idea; motif; objective summary; develop; refine
notes: State a theme as a full sentence about people or life (never one word) and trace how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details over the course of a text; write an objective summary with no opinion. Grade 8 tied theme to characters, setting and plot; 9-10 asks how the theme emerges and is refined detail by detail, so students mark the first hint, the turn and the closing image. Practised on short stories and on Romeo and Juliet. Grade 9 limit: one theme per text, traced at three to four points, with a summary of about 100 words checked for opinion words. Grade 10 handles two themes in tension across a novel.

words: complex character; motivation; conflicting motives; foil; interaction; advance the plot
notes: Analyze how a character with more than one motive, or motives at war, develops, how they act on other characters and how that moves the plot or builds the theme. Grade 8 asked how a line of dialogue or an incident propels action or reveals character; 9-10 widens to the whole arc of a complex character. Practised on short stories and the play: Juliet, Romeo, Friar Laurence and the Nurse are the year's main case. Grade 9 limit: one complex character at a time, with a two-column motive chart (what they want, what pulls against it) at three scenes. Teacher note: Romeo and Juliet ends in two suicides; the unit names this before reading, treats it as the play's tragedy and not as a choice to admire, and gives the school's support contacts.

words: connotation; figurative meaning; tone; diction; euphemism; oxymoron; imagery
notes: Work out what words mean as used, including figurative and connotative meanings, and say how a word choice sets tone or a sense of time and place. RL.9-10.4 adds to grade 8 the cumulative impact of many choices; grade 9 begins with the single choice and pairs of choices, and grade 10 owns the cumulative case. L.9-10.5 adds the new figures (euphemism, oxymoron; grade 8 had verbal irony and puns) and nuance among words of like meaning; Romeo and Juliet's oxymorons and the short stories' euphemisms are the practice. Practised on poems (sonnets, ballads, public-domain lyric poems of 14 to 40 lines) and on key passages of the year's stories.

words: pacing; flashback; foreshadowing; suspense; tension; parallel plot; frame
notes: Analyze how an author's choices about structure, the order of events and the handling of time (pacing, flashback, foreshadowing, parallel plots) create mystery, tension or surprise. Grade 8 compared the structures of two texts; 9-10 moves inside one text to name the choice and its effect on a reader. Practised on suspense and twist stories of 2,000 to 6,000 words (Poe, Saki, Bierce's flashback story) and on the play's compressed four days. Grade 9 limit: one structural choice and one named effect per analysis; grade 10 weighs several choices across a novel.

words: source material; allusion; retelling; transform; epic; artistic medium
cross_subject: social-studies:ss7-greek-myth (Greek gods and heroes met in grade 7 history, ELA supplies the epic)
notes: Trace how a later work draws on and changes older source material, and compare one subject in two artistic mediums. Grade 8 asked how a modern story draws on myth and renders it new; RL.9-10.9 names a specific work and its source, and grade 9 practises on the Odyssey (a public-domain prose translation, books read whole and in large parts) set beside later poems that answer it (for example Tennyson's Ulysses). RL.9-10.7 starts here: Ovid's Icarus story in translation beside Brueghel's painting of the fall of Icarus, asking what each emphasizes or leaves out. Grade 10 owns both, on Shakespeare and his sources.

words: point of view; cultural experience; translation; setting; world literature
notes: Analyze a point of view or cultural experience in a story written outside the United States. Grade 8 asked about differences in point of view between characters and reader; RL.9-10.6 turns to the culture a work comes from and asks for wide reading of world literature. Grade 9 starts with four to six short stories in public-domain translation from several regions (for example Chekhov, Maupassant, Tagore, a story from the Odyssey's world of guest and host), with a short background note before reading only where the text does not supply it. Grade 9 limit: one story at a time; grade 10 compares across works and adds a longer work.

words: drama; act; scene; soliloquy; aside; sonnet; stanza; epic
notes: Read and understand stories, a whole play and poems in the grades 9-10 band, with scaffolding at the high end (the standard's own end-of-grade-9 line). The year's long texts read whole: Romeo and Juliet (every scene, with audio beside the text and the long-sentence routine for verse) and the Odyssey in prose translation in large parts. Reading volume and a log of a long on-topic book each unit sit here. Text demand for English 9: anchors in the grades 9-10 band (2012 supplement to Appendix A: about 1050 to 1335 Lexile), most placed in the lower two thirds, with scaffolding at the high end; a poem or play has no usable measure and rests on the qualitative read. Grade 10 removes the scaffolding: independent at the high end.

words: central idea; objective summary; literary nonfiction; refine; textual evidence
notes: Cite thorough evidence from nonfiction, find a central idea and show how it emerges and is refined by specific details, and summarize objectively. Grade 8 related the central idea to supporting ideas; 9-10 asks how it is shaped and refined as the text goes. Practised on literary nonfiction of 1,000 to 4,000 words tied to the year's topic sets: essays and memoir passages on journeys and exile beside the Odyssey, and essays on science and risk. RI.9-10.10 here: proficient with scaffolding at the high end. Text demand for English 9: anchors in the grades 9-10 band (2012 supplement to Appendix A: about 1050 to 1335 Lexile), most placed in the lower two thirds, with scaffolding at the high end; a poem or play has no usable measure and rests on the qualitative read.

words: sequence of ideas; connection; distinction; transition; section; technical term
cross_subject: science:HS-LS4-1 (reading an explanation of the evidence for common ancestry in grade 9 biology)
notes: Analyze how an author unfolds a series of ideas or events (the order of points, how each is introduced and developed, the connections drawn) and how particular sentences and paragraphs develop a claim. Grade 8 looked at the role of sentences in one paragraph; RI.9-10.5 widens to larger portions (a section or chapter) and RI.9-10.3 to the whole line of an analysis. RI.9-10.4 starts with technical and connotative words in context. Practised on explanatory science and history essays of 1,500 to 3,000 words with headings. Grade 9 limit: a two-level outline of one text's moves; grade 10 compares how two authors order the same material.

words: rhetoric; purpose; audience; occasion; appeal; ethos; pathos; logos; repetition
cross_subject: social-studies:ss8-declaration (the Declaration read as a founding document in grade 8)
notes: Determine a speaker's point of view or purpose and analyze how rhetoric advances it. Grade 8 asked how an author answers conflicting viewpoints; 9-10 adds rhetoric as a set of named moves. Extends the rhetorical-situation model (speaker, audience, purpose, occasion, in use since grade 4 and applied to reading since grade 6) by adding the three appeals as the year's tool. Practised on short speeches of 250 to 2,000 words; grade 9 starts RI.9-10.9 with two seminal U.S. documents read closely, the Gettysburg Address and an excerpt of Washington's Farewell Address, for how they address union. Grade 10 owns the full set across a theme. Grade 9 limit: name the move and its effect on this audience.

words: claim; reason; valid; relevant; sufficient; fallacy; false statement
cross_subject: math:S-ID.C.9 (correlation is not causation, the commonest fallacy in data claims)
notes: Lay out an argument's claims and judge whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence relevant and sufficient; spot false statements and fallacious reasoning. Grade 8 judged soundness and spotted irrelevant evidence; 9-10 adds validity and named fallacies. Grade 9 teaches a short set of fallacies (hasty generalization, false cause, either-or, attack on the person) on op-ed style essays and letters of 600 to 1,500 words, mapped as claim, reasons and evidence. SL.9-10.3 starts on a recorded speech judged the same way. Grade 10 adds the full judgment on longer arguments. Math lean: S-ID.C.9 is taught in Algebra 1, grade 9 (alg1-correlation-causation in the math progression). If this unit comes before that math in the year, the ELA lesson supplies the display, a worked interpretation and the correlation versus causation distinction, and does not assume the math is done.

words: medium; account; emphasis; omission; multimedia; credibility
cross_subject: social-studies:wh1-graphic-displays (reading maps, charts and timelines as information)
notes: Compare accounts of one subject in different mediums and say which details each emphasizes. Grade 8 weighed the advantages of mediums in general; 9-10 compares named accounts of one subject. Grade 9 practises on a person's life story told in a print memoir passage and in a short documentary or audio piece (public-domain government film or an original Curio Class recording). SL.9-10.2 starts: combine information from a chart, a talk and a text, asking how credible and accurate each is. Grade 10 adds data displays and judged source sets.

words: analytic paragraph; topic sentence; embedded quotation; commentary; on-demand
notes: Write routinely from texts: analytic paragraphs that state a reading, embed evidence and explain it, plus short on-demand responses in one sitting. W.9-10.9a and 9b apply the grade's reading standards; grade 8 named the same habit at grade 8 demand. Grade 9 builds the analytic paragraph (claim, two quotations, commentary longer than the quotations) to fluency, then joins paragraphs into a short essay; the frame fades by the second semester. The daily exit question is part of this row. Grade 10 moves to the full analytic essay, timed and untimed.

words: explain; extended definition; concrete detail; transition; formal style; implication
cross_subject: science:HS-LS2-7 (explaining a human impact on an ecosystem in grade 9 biology)
notes: Write explanatory pieces that make complex ideas clear: introduce the topic, organize to show connections and distinctions, develop with facts, extended definitions and quotations, use varied transitions and precise words, and close by saying why it matters. Grade 8 asked to examine a topic; 9-10 asks to examine complex ideas and adds extended definitions and implications. Grade 9: one process piece (about 800 to 1,200 words) on a topic set from the year's nonfiction, with a model piece and a rubric used all year, plus short explanations. Grade 10 adds graphics and headings by choice and a longer sourced piece.

words: precise claim; counterclaim; rebuttal; cohesion; objective tone; concluding section
cross_subject: social-studies:wh1-historical-argument (claims with evidence from sources in grade 9 world history)
notes: Write arguments on texts and issues with a precise claim, reasons, relevant evidence, a counterclaim and a response, cohesive links and a formal, objective tone. Grade 8 acknowledged opposing claims; 9-10 asks the writer to distinguish them and organize the relations among claim, counterclaim, reasons and evidence. Grade 9 takes W.9-10.1a, c, d and e in full and starts 1b with one counterclaim answered fairly; two process arguments a year (a literary argument and an issue argument from a nonfiction set, 800 to 1,200 words) with a model piece. Grade 10 adds several counterclaims weighed by strengths and limits for a named audience.

words: narrator; point of view; pacing; reflection; telling detail; sensory language
notes: Write narratives, real or imagined, that set out a problem or situation, establish a point of view, move smoothly through events, use dialogue, pacing, description and reflection, and close on what was learned or resolved. Grade 8 established context and point of view; 9-10 adds multiple points of view and plot lines and events that build to a coherent whole. Grade 9: one process narrative (a personal narrative or a story that answers the Odyssey or a short story read) of 1,000 to 1,500 words, with one point of view and one plot line, and short scene-writing from the stories' techniques. Grade 10 adds two points of view or plot lines.

words: task; purpose; audience; revise; edit; peer response; publish
notes: Run the writing process: plan, draft, revise, edit, rewrite or try a new approach, keeping task, purpose and audience in view; produce, publish and update typed work. Grade 8 did this 'with some guidance and support from peers and adults'; 9-10 drops that phrase and asks the writer to judge what is most significant to fix. Grade 9 still runs a structured peer response and a named teacher feedback step on every process piece, and students keep a revision log naming the one biggest change. W.9-10.6: typed, shared and updated where devices allow; a room without them hand-writes and publishes on a class wall, which does not demonstrate W.9-10.6; the typed, published and updated piece is made on a shared device or in a lab session in the school day, or the requirement is recorded as unfinished. Grade 10 makes revision choices independent.

words: research question; advanced search; authoritative; usefulness; paraphrase; plagiarism; works cited
cross_subject: social-studies:wh1-inquiry-questions (drafting supporting questions for an inquiry in grade 9)
notes: Run short research projects (three to five days) that answer a question, including a student's own, narrowing or broadening it as sources come in, and combine several sources. Grade 8 ran short projects with several sources and judged credibility; 9-10 adds advanced searches, judging each source's usefulness for this question, integrating quotations selectively and a standard citation format from a style manual (L.9-10.3a starts here). Grade 9: two short projects tied to the year's topic sets, each ending in a cited short paper or talk. Grade 10 adds one sustained project. Choice of style manual: see the lead list.

words: seminar; norm; prepared; build on; clarify; challenge; qualify
notes: Take part in discussions of texts and issues, prepared with marked evidence, building on others and saying one's own view clearly and persuasively. Grade 8 followed rules for discussion; SL.9-10.1b has students set the rules, goals and roles themselves, and 1c and 1d add relating the talk to larger ideas, drawing others in and summarizing agreement and disagreement. Grade 9: a whole-class text discussion at least twice a unit on the anchor, with the class writing its own norms in unit 1 and sentence frames that fade; partner talk daily. Grade 10 runs student-led seminars.

words: line of reasoning; concise; visual aid; formal register; audience
notes: Present findings with evidence so listeners can follow the line of reasoning, use digital media with purpose, and shift into formal English when the task asks. Grade 8 presented claims with eye contact and volume; 9-10 asks for organization and style fitted to purpose and audience, and strategic media. Grade 9: a three to five minute talk from each short research project and a recited or performed passage of the play (practised rereading aloud), with a look-for sheet. Grade 10 adds a longer talk with questions from the audience.

words: phrase; clause; participial phrase; absolute phrase; relative clause; parallel structure
notes: Use the kinds of phrases (noun, verb, adjectival, adverbial, participial, prepositional, absolute) and clauses (independent, dependent; noun, relative, adverbial) to say exactly what is meant and to vary sentences. Grade 8 explained verbals; grade 9 builds participial and absolute phrases from them. Taught by combining sentences from the anchor texts and from students' drafts, never as grammar on its own. Grade 9 takes L.9-10.1b and introduces parallel structure (1a) on lists; grade 10 owns parallel structure in longer sentences and uses both for style.

words: semicolon; conjunctive adverb; independent clause; comma splice; spelling
notes: Use a semicolon, with or without a conjunctive adverb (however, therefore), to join closely related independent clauses, and spell correctly. Grade 8 punctuated pauses and omissions; 9-10 adds the semicolon and the colon. Grade 9 takes L.9-10.2a and 2c, practised in editing students' own drafts and in fixing comma splices; the colon for quotations (2b) belongs to grade 10, where quotations are integrated into analysis. Language Progressive Skills from earlier grades (fragments, run-ons, pronoun agreement) are checked in the same editing step.

words: word family; derivation; etymology; part of speech; verify; general academic word
notes: Work out unknown and multiple-meaning words from context, word changes (analyze, analysis, analytical) and reference works, then check the guess. Grade 8 used Greek and Latin roots; 9-10 adds patterns of word change across parts of speech and etymology in the dictionary. Each unit's word list comes from its texts, mostly general academic words, met before, during and after reading and returned to later. Grade 9 limit: the class learns 10 to 15 words in depth per unit; grade 10 adds the student's own word log for independence (L.9-10.6).

words: textual evidence; thorough; inference; ambiguity; weigh
notes: Owns RL.9-10.1. Cite strong and thorough evidence across a whole novel and a whole play, including where the text leaves things uncertain. Grade 9 gathered two or three quotations per claim in a story, with a chart; grade 10 tracks evidence across chapters, chooses among competing pieces and says why one is stronger, with no chart. Practised on Frankenstein (1818 text, read whole) and Julius Caesar. Text demand for English 10: anchors reach the high end of the grades 9-10 band (about 1185 to 1335 Lexile and the hardest older prose), read independently by year's end; poems and plays rest on the qualitative read.

words: theme; motif; tension; refine; objective summary
notes: Owns RL.9-10.2. Determine themes and analyze in detail how they emerge and are refined across a long text, and write an objective summary of a whole novel or play. Grade 9 traced one theme in a story or the play at a few points; grade 10 follows two themes that pull against each other (creation and responsibility in Frankenstein, honor and ambition in Julius Caesar) through motifs, and summarizes a book-length text in about 200 words.

words: complex character; motivation; foil; interaction; develop; tragic flaw
notes: Owns RL.9-10.3. Analyze how complex characters with conflicting motives develop over a long text, interact and advance the plot or theme. Grade 9 charted one character at a few scenes; grade 10 follows pairs of characters who shape each other (Victor and the creature, Brutus and Cassius) across the whole work. Teacher note: Frankenstein includes murders and deaths of family members, and Julius Caesar an assassination and suicides; name them before reading and treat them through the works' own judgment.

words: cumulative impact; tone; diction; connotation; nuance; euphemism; oxymoron
notes: Owns RL.9-10.4 and L.9-10.5. Analyze the cumulative impact of many word choices on meaning and tone across a passage, a speech or a poem (how the language builds a time and place, a formal or informal tone). Grade 9 named single choices and pairs; grade 10 tracks a pattern of diction through a whole poem or speech and explains its total effect. L.9-10.5: interpret figures of speech in their role in the text, and the nuance between words with like denotations. Practised on Antony's and Brutus's funeral speeches and on a poetry set (public-domain poems, 14 to 60 lines).

words: frame narrative; nested narrator; pacing; parallel plot; manipulate time; effect
notes: Owns RL.9-10.5. Analyze several structural choices working together across a long text and the effects they create. Grade 9 named one choice and one effect in a short story; grade 10 weighs the whole build of a novel (Frankenstein's nested frame narratives, letters and the creature's story inside Victor's) and of a play's acts, with suspense, mystery and surprise each traced to a choice.

words: world literature; cultural experience; point of view; translation; tradition
cross_subject: social-studies:wh2-imperialism-impact (stories written under colonial rule, read beside the history)
notes: Owns RL.9-10.6. Analyze a point of view or cultural experience in works from outside the United States, drawing on a wide reading of world literature. Grade 9 read single short stories in translation; grade 10 reads a longer work (for example a Greek tragedy such as Antigone in a public-domain translation) and a set of stories and poems from at least three regions, comparing how each reflects its culture. Teacher note: the range of public-domain translations leans to older European and South Asian work; see the lead list.

words: source material; adaptation; transform; artistic medium; emphasis; absence
cross_subject: social-studies:ss7-republic-to-empire (Julius Caesar and the end of the Republic in grade 7 history)
notes: Owns RL.9-10.9 and RL.9-10.7. Analyze how an author draws on and transforms source material in a specific work: Shakespeare's Julius Caesar beside passages of Plutarch's life of Caesar (public-domain translation), what he kept, cut and invented. Grade 9 compared the Odyssey with later poems that answer it; grade 10 compares line by line against a named source. RL.9-10.7: a key scene in two artistic mediums (the assassination in the play and in a nineteenth-century painting, or a staged recording), saying what each emphasizes or leaves out. History supplies the context (Caesar and the end of the Republic, grade 7); ELA supplies and teaches the Plutarch passages and the comparison.

words: novel; tragedy; verse; prose; independent reading
notes: Owns RL.9-10.10. By the end of grade 10, read stories, plays and poems at the high end of the 9-10 band independently and proficiently (the standard's own end-of-grade-10 line; grade 9 had scaffolding at the high end). Long texts read whole: Frankenstein and Julius Caesar; routine scaffolds, the long-sentence routine among them, fade through the year as students show readiness, with independent reading checkpoints at the high end of the band; targeted instruction and access supports continue where needed, and supported reading is kept apart from evidence of independent proficiency. Independent reading of a long on-topic book each unit with a log and a conference. Text demand for English 10: anchors reach the high end of the grades 9-10 band (about 1185 to 1335 Lexile and the hardest older prose), read independently by year's end; poems and plays rest on the qualitative read.

words: central idea; refine; objective summary; literary nonfiction; thorough evidence
notes: Owns RI.9-10.1, RI.9-10.2 and RI.9-10.10. Cite thorough evidence, trace a central idea through a long essay or a chapter of nonfiction, and summarize objectively. Grade 9 did this on essays of up to 4,000 words with scaffolding; grade 10 reads longer and denser nonfiction (science writing beside Frankenstein, on making life and its limits; nineteenth-century essays) at the high end of the band independently by year's end. Text demand for English 10: anchors reach the high end of the grades 9-10 band (about 1185 to 1335 Lexile and the hardest older prose), read independently by year's end; poems and plays rest on the qualitative read.

words: line of reasoning; section; refine; connection; order of points
notes: Owns RI.9-10.3 and RI.9-10.5. Analyze how an author orders and develops a series of ideas and how particular sentences, paragraphs and sections develop and refine claims. Grade 9 outlined one text's moves; grade 10 compares how two authors order the same material (two explanations of one scientific discovery, two accounts of one event) and why. Practised on essays and chapters of 2,000 to 5,000 words.

words: technical meaning; connotation; register; cumulative impact; tone
notes: Owns RI.9-10.4. Determine figurative, connotative and technical meanings and analyze the cumulative impact of word choices on meaning and tone, as in how the language of a court opinion differs from a newspaper's. Grade 9 worked out technical words in explanatory essays; grade 10 compares register across texts on one event (a public-domain court opinion or official report beside a news account of it).

words: rhetoric; purpose; audience; appeal; propaganda; rhetorical question; parallelism
cross_subject: social-studies:wh2-totalitarian-regimes (propaganda studied in grade 10 world history)
notes: Owns RI.9-10.6. Determine an author's point of view or purpose and analyze how rhetoric advances it across a whole speech or essay. Grade 9 named single moves and their effect; grade 10 explains how the moves work together for an audience and judges whether they serve or manipulate the reader, including wartime speeches beside propaganda. Practised on speeches and essays of 1,000 to 4,000 words.

words: seminal document; founding; liberty; address; related theme
cross_subject: social-studies:ss8-constitution-text (the founding documents read in grade 8 civics)
notes: Owns RI.9-10.9. Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance and how they address related themes. Grade 9 read two short documents closely for their rhetoric; grade 10 reads a set on one theme (liberty and who it includes: the Declaration of Independence, the Declaration of Sentiments, Susan B. Anthony's 1873 speech on her arrest for voting, Chief Joseph's 1879 Washington address asking to live as a free man, Roosevelt's Four Freedoms speech) and compares how each takes up the theme. Douglass's July Fifth speech is read in grade 11 (e11-info-rhetoric) and Lincoln's Second Inaugural, which RI.11-12.9 names, in grade 11 (e11-info-founding-documents), so neither is in this set. Teacher note: Chief Joseph's address describes the Nez Perce removal and the deaths it caused; prepare the class and keep the focus on his argument. The standard's own example of King's letter is not public domain; see the lead list.

words: valid; sufficient; fallacy; exaggerated evidence; distorted evidence; premise
cross_subject: math:8.SP.A.1 (patterns of association in data)
notes: Owns RI.9-10.8 and SL.9-10.3. Delineate and evaluate a full argument: is the reasoning valid, is the evidence relevant and sufficient, where are false statements and fallacies. Grade 9 mapped short op-eds and named four fallacies; grade 10 maps long arguments with several lines of reasoning, adds fallacies of data and authority, and writes a judgment of the whole. SL.9-10.3 owns the same on a speaker: point of view, reasoning, rhetoric, exaggerated or distorted evidence, on recorded public-domain speeches and debates. Math lean: S-IC.B.6 (evaluating reports based on data) is owned in grade 11 in the math progression (alg2-experiments-significance), so this row leans on the grade 8 scatter-plot work instead; fallacies of data stay with association and correlation, and anything beyond is supplied by the ELA lesson.

words: account; medium; emphasis; credibility; accuracy; data display
cross_subject: math:8.SP.A.1 (reading scatter plots and patterns of association)
notes: Owns RI.9-10.7 and SL.9-10.2. Analyze accounts of one subject in different mediums, deciding which details each emphasizes, and integrate several sources (visual, numeric, spoken) while judging each for credibility and accuracy. Grade 9 compared a print and a filmed life story; grade 10 works a source set of five or more items on one topic (a report, a graph, a recorded talk, a news piece), as the base of the sustained research project.

words: counterclaim; strengths and limitations; audience; cohesion; formal style; qualify
cross_subject: social-studies:wh2-historians-interpretations (weighing competing interpretations in grade 10 world history)
notes: Owns W.9-10.1 with all of a to e. Write arguments that develop claims and counterclaims fairly, with evidence for each and their strengths and limits, for an audience whose knowledge and concerns the writer anticipates. Grade 9 answered one counterclaim; grade 10 weighs several and may qualify its own claim, in two process arguments (literary and issue, 1,200 to 1,800 words) and timed arguments. Writing shares across the two years lean toward about 40 percent argument, 40 informative and 20 narrative, the grade 12 shares the standards' introduction gives for writing across all subjects, not ELA alone; Curio Class uses them as ELA planning guidance, and the review criteria report ELA process-writing distributions separately.

words: complex idea; extended definition; formatting; graphic; domain vocabulary; implication
cross_subject: science:HS-ESS3-5 (explaining what climate data and forecasts show, in grade 10 science)
notes: Owns W.9-10.2 with all of a to f. Write explanations of complex ideas with headings, figures or tables where they help, sourced facts and quotations, varied transitions, domain words and a close that draws out implications. Grade 9 wrote a process explanation without graphics; grade 10 writes a longer sourced explanatory piece (1,200 to 1,800 words) with at least one figure or table the writer makes, and short explanations across units.

words: multiple points of view; plot line; pacing; reflection; coherent whole
notes: Owns W.9-10.3 with all of a to e. Write narratives with more than one point of view or plot line, sequenced so events build into a coherent whole, with telling detail and a reflective close. Grade 9 kept one point of view and one line; grade 10 writes one process narrative (for example a story told by two narrators, in answer to Frankenstein's nested tellings, 1,500 to 2,000 words) and narrative passages inside other writing.

words: revise; significant; audience; publish; update; shared document
notes: Owns W.9-10.4, W.9-10.5 and W.9-10.6. Produce clear, coherent writing fitted to task, purpose and audience and revise independently for what matters most. Grade 9 used a structured peer response and teacher step; grade 10 students set their own revision goal from the rubric and judge their changes, and the teacher step becomes a conference. W.9-10.6: publish and update a shared or linked product (the research project's page or document, with links to sources); the plan says what a room without devices does.

words: sustained research; synthesize; narrow; broaden; usefulness; integrate; works cited
cross_subject: social-studies:wh2-research-argument (a researched argument in grade 10 world history)
notes: Owns W.9-10.7 and W.9-10.8. Run short projects and one sustained project (about three weeks) that answers a self-generated question, narrowing or broadening as needed, synthesizing many sources, with advanced searches, a judgment of each source's usefulness, selective quotation and a full citation form. Grade 9 ran two short projects; grade 10 adds the sustained one and synthesis across sources that disagree. Applies L.9-10.3a, following a style manual's format; e10-l-syntax-style owns L.9-10.3. Where a school teaches both courses, one project may serve both: the course frames write one shared brief, and each course still teaches the whole cycle for schools that use it alone.

words: literary analysis; thesis; embedded quotation; commentary; timed writing
notes: Owns W.9-10.9 and W.9-10.10. Draw evidence from literature and nonfiction to support full analytic essays, applying the grade's reading standards (9a, for example Shakespeare's use of Plutarch; 9b, judging an argument), and write routinely over long and short time frames. Grade 9 built the analytic paragraph and a short essay; grade 10 writes the multi-paragraph analytic essay with a thesis, both through the process and in one timed sitting, plus the daily exit question.

words: student-led seminar; consensus; propel; diverse perspectives; qualify; synthesize
notes: Owns SL.9-10.1 with all of a to d. Run student-led discussions: students prepare from texts and research, set their own rules and roles, propel the talk with questions that tie it to larger ideas, bring others in, and summarize agreement and disagreement, qualifying their views. Grade 9 discussions were teacher-led with fading frames; grade 10 hands leading to students, with the teacher observing against a look-for sheet, at least twice a unit on the anchor.

words: line of reasoning; substance; digital media; formal English; audience questions
notes: Owns SL.9-10.4, SL.9-10.5 and SL.9-10.6. Present findings clearly and concisely with a line of reasoning the audience can follow, use digital media strategically, and adapt speech to context. Grade 9 gave short talks from short projects; grade 10 presents the sustained research project (8 to 10 minutes with questions from the audience) and performs a speech from Julius Caesar, judged on the same look-for sheet.

words: parallel structure; phrase; clause; style; register; style manual
notes: Owns L.9-10.1 and L.9-10.3. Use parallel structure (a Language Progressive Skill, checked in later grades too) and the full range of phrases and clauses to convey meaning and add variety, and apply knowledge of language to make choices for meaning or style and to read more fully. Grade 9 built the phrase and clause types; grade 10 studies parallelism in the year's speeches (Lincoln, Antony) and imitates it, and edits to a style manual (L.9-10.3a, applied in research writing). Taught through sentences from the anchors and from drafts.

words: colon; quotation; semicolon; list; spelling
notes: Owns L.9-10.2 with all of a to c. Use a colon to introduce a list or a quotation, keep the semicolon from grade 9 in use, and spell correctly. Grade 9 taught the semicolon; grade 10 adds the colon, practised where it is needed most, in introducing quotations in analytic essays and research writing, and edits drafts for all three.

words: word family; etymology; verify; reference; general academic word; domain word
notes: Owns L.9-10.4 and L.9-10.6. Choose flexibly among context, word changes and reference works to settle a word's meaning, verify it, and gather words independently. Grade 9 taught the strategies on the unit word list; grade 10 has students keep their own log of words important to understanding and use them in writing and talk, on top of a unit list of 10 to 15 words met before, during and after reading and returned to later.

words: ambiguity; inference; explicit; textual evidence; uncertain; competing reading
notes: Cite strong and thorough evidence for what a text says and implies, and name where the text leaves a matter uncertain. Practised on short American stories built on doubt (Hawthorne's 'Young Goodman Brown', Bierce's 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge', Poe's 'The Fall of the House of Usher'; 3,000 to 8,000 words each, 18th and 19th century prose, high qualitative demand from older syntax and allusion) and, for RI, Douglass's Narrative (1845).
